title: A Quiet Novel of Large Ambitions
text:
The novel under review is a first book, and it has many of the virtues and a few of the faults of first books. Its setting is a small fishing town on a southern coast, where the arrival of a large processing plant threatens the livelihoods of families who have worked the same waters for generations. Over roughly a year, we follow three members of one such family: a father who refuses to sell his boat, a daughter who takes a job at the plant, and a grandmother whose memories of earlier hardships give the story its depth.

The author’s great strength is her eye for detail. The smell of drying nets, the arguments over the price of diesel, the particular silence of a house after a quarrel: all of these are rendered with a precision that makes the town feel inhabited rather than invented. She is also admirably fair to her characters. The daughter’s decision to work at the plant is presented not as betrayal but as a reasonable response to debt, and even the plant’s manager, who might easily have been a villain, is allowed moments of doubt.

The weaknesses lie mainly in the structure. The middle section drifts, with several chapters that add atmosphere but little movement, and a subplot involving a visiting journalist is introduced with some fanfare only to be abandoned. The ending, by contrast, feels hurried, as though the author had suddenly remembered that a story must conclude.

These are real flaws, but they are the flaws of a writer still learning to manage a large canvas, not of one who lacks talent. Readers who value plot above all may grow impatient. Those who are content to live for a while inside a vividly observed world, and to watch ordinary people make difficult choices, will find the book rewarding, and will look forward to what its author does next.

title: Bringing Government Closer
text:
Few ideas in public administration enjoy such broad support as decentralisation. Politicians of very different views agree that decisions about schools, water supply, sanitation and local roads are better made close to the people they affect than in a distant capital. Local officials, the argument runs, know local conditions, and citizens can more easily hold accountable those whom they meet in the street.

The argument is sound as far as it goes, but experience suggests that transferring authority is only the beginning. Local governments need money as well as powers, and when responsibilities are handed down without the revenue to meet them, the result is frustration rather than empowerment. A district council that is legally responsible for clinics but depends entirely on unpredictable grants from above cannot plan, and its failures are blamed on decentralisation itself.

Capacity is a second difficulty. Managing budgets, awarding contracts and supervising staff require skills that newly created local bodies may lack. Without training and clear rules, decentralisation can simply move opportunities for favouritism from the capital to the district, where they may be even harder to detect. Local elites, well connected and well organised, are often better placed than ordinary citizens to dominate the new institutions.

Finally, decentralisation depends on continuity. Local governments that are dissolved, suspended or reorganised every few years never accumulate experience or public trust. Citizens learn that it is pointless to engage with bodies that may not exist by the next election.

None of these problems is an argument for returning all power to the centre. They are reminders that decentralisation is not a single act but a long process, requiring reliable finance, patient investment in skills, transparent procedures and, above all, the political willingness to let local institutions survive long enough to prove their worth.

title: What Inflation Does
text:
Inflation is usually described as a rise in the general level of prices, but its effects are better understood as a fall in the purchasing power of money. When prices rise steadily, the same banknote buys a little less each month. A modest and predictable rate of inflation is generally regarded as manageable, even helpful, because it gives businesses room to adjust and discourages people from hoarding cash. It is high and unpredictable inflation that does the damage.

That damage is not shared equally. Households whose incomes are fixed in money terms, such as pensioners and workers whose wages are revised only occasionally, find their living standards eroded between one adjustment and the next. Those who hold their savings in cash see the value quietly drain away. By contrast, borrowers may gain, since the debts they owe shrink in real terms, and people who own property or other assets whose prices rise with inflation are partly protected. For this reason economists sometimes describe inflation as a hidden tax, one that falls most heavily on those least able to shield themselves.

Uncertainty adds a further cost. When no one knows what prices will be next year, businesses hesitate to invest, lenders demand higher interest to compensate for the risk, and long-term contracts become difficult to write. Time and energy that might be spent producing goods are spent instead on protecting oneself against rising prices.

Controlling inflation is therefore a central task of economic policy, usually entrusted to a central bank that can raise interest rates to cool spending. But the remedy has its own price. Higher rates slow borrowing and investment and can increase unemployment for a time. The art of monetary policy lies in restraining prices without inflicting more harm than the inflation itself would have caused.

title: The Monsoon and the Sea Roads
text:
For centuries before steam replaced sail, the trade of the Indian Ocean moved to a rhythm set by the winds. Over much of the ocean the prevailing winds reverse direction with the seasons, blowing from the south-west for part of the year and from the north-east for another. Sailors who understood this pattern could travel long distances with confidence, sailing out on one monsoon and returning on the next.

This regularity shaped the character of the trade. Because a merchant might have to wait months in a foreign port for the wind to change, ports became places of long residence rather than brief visits. Traders settled, married, built places of worship and learned local languages, and communities of merchants from distant lands became a familiar feature of coastal towns from East Africa to South-East Asia. Along with textiles, spices, timber and precious metals, the ships carried religious ideas, legal customs, words and recipes.

The monsoon system also encouraged a network of connected voyages rather than single journeys from one end of the ocean to the other. Goods were often carried in stages, changing hands in intermediate ports, so that a bale of cloth might pass through several merchants before reaching its final buyer. For much of this long period no single power controlled the whole ocean; the trade was sustained by a web of merchants, rulers and port cities, each with an interest in keeping goods moving.

Historians have come to see this maritime world as one of the great zones of exchange in human history, comparable in importance to the overland routes that are more familiar to many readers. Its legacy is still visible in the mixed vocabularies of coastal languages, in the architecture of old port towns and in the family histories of communities whose ancestors arrived with the wind.

subject: English
q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: summarise the history of a fishing town
argue against the building of processing plants
assess the strengths and weaknesses of a first novel
compare several novels about the sea
explanation: The passage is a book review: it outlines the story, praises the author’s detail and fairness, identifies structural flaws and gives an overall judgement.

subject: English
q: According to the reviewer, the author’s great strength is:
o: her fast-moving plot
her use of humour
her precise observation of detail
her portrayal of the journalist
explanation: The second paragraph begins, ‘The author’s great strength is her eye for detail’, and gives examples such as the smell of drying nets.

subject: English
q: The word ‘fanfare’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: a show of importance
careful planning
loud music
great secrecy
explanation: A subplot ‘introduced with some fanfare only to be abandoned’ is one presented as if it would matter a great deal; the literal sense of a trumpet flourish does not apply.

subject: English
q: The reviewer would most likely recommend the novel to readers who:
o: want a tightly plotted thriller
are interested mainly in the economics of fishing
prefer stories with clear heroes and villains
enjoy close observation of character and setting more than fast action
explanation: The last paragraph warns that plot-minded readers ‘may grow impatient’ but says those content to live inside ‘a vividly observed world’ will find it rewarding; the book also avoids simple villains.

subject: English
q: The remark that the ending reads ‘as though the author had suddenly remembered that a story must conclude’ implies that the ending:
o: was the most carefully written part of the book
was not adequately prepared for by what came before
left the story deliberately unresolved
repeated the opening scene of the novel
explanation: After a drifting middle, the conclusion ‘feels hurried’; the image of a sudden remembering suggests it arrives abruptly without the groundwork the story needed.

subject: English
q: The reviewer’s overall attitude towards the novel is best described as:
o: appreciative, with reservations
wholly enthusiastic
largely dismissive
neutral and indifferent
explanation: The reviewer praises the book’s detail and fairness and calls it rewarding, but also lists ‘real flaws’ in its structure.

subject: English
q: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
o: Decentralisation has failed wherever it has been tried
All important decisions should be made by the central government
Decentralisation succeeds only when it is backed by finance, capacity and continuity
Local elites are the main cause of poor public services
explanation: The author accepts the case for decentralisation but argues that it is ‘a long process’ needing reliable finance, skills, transparent procedures and institutions allowed to survive.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what happens when responsibilities are handed down without revenue?
o: Local elites lose their influence
The result is frustration rather than empowerment
Citizens stop voting in national elections
Clinics are transferred back to the capital
explanation: The second paragraph states that when responsibilities come ‘without the revenue to meet them, the result is frustration rather than empowerment’.

subject: English
q: The passage warns that without training and clear rules, decentralisation may:
o: eliminate corruption entirely
force local councils to raise taxes
make central grants more predictable
shift opportunities for favouritism to the local level
explanation: The third paragraph says decentralisation can then ‘move opportunities for favouritism from the capital to the district, where they may be even harder to detect’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘accumulate’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: lose quickly
build up gradually
share equally
record officially
explanation: Local bodies reorganised every few years ‘never accumulate experience or public trust’ — they never have time to build these up.

subject: English
q: The author would most likely regard a proposal to abolish local governments because they have performed poorly as:
o: sensible, since central government is always more efficient
necessary, since local elites can never be controlled
irrelevant, since local governments have no real powers
mistaken, since poor performance often reflects inadequate support rather than a flawed idea
explanation: The author notes that under-funded councils’ failures ‘are blamed on decentralisation itself’ and insists the problems are ‘not an argument for returning all power to the centre’.

subject: English
q: The tone of the passage is best described as:
o: measured and constructive
bitterly hostile
naively optimistic
detached and indifferent
explanation: The author weighs the idea’s merits against its practical difficulties and ends with the conditions needed for success, neither rejecting it nor overlooking its problems.

subject: English
q: The passage is primarily about:
o: the history of central banking
why property prices always rise
the effects of inflation and the difficulty of controlling it
how pensions are calculated
explanation: The passage explains who is harmed by inflation, the costs of uncertainty, and the trade-offs a central bank faces in restraining prices.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, which group may actually gain from inflation?
o: Pensioners
People who save in cash
Borrowers
Workers whose wages are rarely revised
explanation: The second paragraph says ‘borrowers may gain, since the debts they owe shrink in real terms’; the other groups are named as losers.

subject: English
q: The word ‘eroded’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: gradually worn away
suddenly increased
officially reviewed
fairly distributed
explanation: Living standards ‘eroded between one adjustment and the next’ are slowly worn down as fixed incomes buy less and less.

subject: English
q: Inflation is described as a ‘hidden tax’ because it:
o: is collected secretly by the central bank
applies only to property owners
is added to the price of imported goods
reduces people’s real wealth without any formal decision to tax them
explanation: Like a tax, inflation takes real value from savers and fixed-income earners, but it does so quietly through rising prices rather than through any declared levy.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why do lenders demand higher interest when inflation is unpredictable?
o: Because the central bank requires them to
To compensate for the risk created by uncertainty
Because borrowers always lose from inflation
To discourage people from hoarding cash
explanation: The third paragraph says that under uncertainty ‘lenders demand higher interest to compensate for the risk’.

subject: English
q: Which of the following statements would the author most likely accept?
o: Raising interest rates to fight inflation involves costs that must be weighed carefully
Any level of inflation, however small, is harmful
A central bank can control inflation without affecting employment
Inflation harms borrowers more than savers
explanation: The last paragraph says the remedy ‘has its own price’, including slower investment and higher unemployment, and must not inflict more harm than the inflation itself.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is the best title for the passage?
o: The Coming of the Steamship
The Spice Trade of a Single Empire
Winds of Exchange: Trade in the Indian Ocean
Overland Routes of Asia
explanation: The passage explains how seasonal winds shaped Indian Ocean trade and the cultural exchange it carried; it states that no single power controlled the ocean for much of the period.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why did ports become places of long residence?
o: Rulers forbade traders to leave
Merchants often had to wait months for the wind to change
Ships were too slow to cross the ocean
Goods could be sold only at the end of the year
explanation: The second paragraph says that ‘because a merchant might have to wait months in a foreign port for the wind to change’, ports became places of long residence.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, goods in the Indian Ocean trade were often:
o: shipped directly from one end of the ocean to the other
controlled by a single imperial power
exchanged only for precious metals
carried in stages and passed through several merchants
explanation: The third paragraph describes ‘a network of connected voyages rather than single journeys’, with goods ‘changing hands in intermediate ports’.

subject: English
q: The word ‘prevailing’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: strongest possible
most common or dominant
victorious
occasional
explanation: ‘The prevailing winds’ are those that usually blow over the ocean in a given season — the dominant pattern sailors relied on.

subject: English
q: The author mentions that ships carried ‘words and recipes’ in order to show that:
o: sailors were interested mainly in food
merchants kept written records of their voyages
the languages of port towns did not change
the trade involved cultural as well as commercial exchange
explanation: Listed alongside religious ideas and legal customs, words and recipes show that the ships carried culture as well as goods, a point echoed by the ‘mixed vocabularies’ in the last paragraph.

subject: English
q: The author’s reference to overland routes that are ‘more familiar to many readers’ suggests that:
o: the maritime trade has received less popular attention than it deserves
the overland routes carried more goods than the sea
the maritime trade was of little importance
most readers already know the history of the Indian Ocean well
explanation: The author calls the maritime world ‘comparable in importance’ to the overland routes while noting those routes are better known, implying the sea trade is relatively neglected.
